doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: John Lewis and the Modern Jazz Quartet
summary: Katz portrays Lewis as a mentor with an iron will who shaped the MJQ on an Ellington model.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: were misfits, or whatever the word is now, I mean there’s no question. Because the guys out there making it are like in any other field, they’re asserting themselves on some level big time. And the best example I know of that, I was very privileged to have a front row seat to John Lewis and the MJQ because he was sort of my mentor, teacher, I used to go stay with him and my whole history with him would make an interview.
Hopefully somebody will do a book on him.

Yeah. They will. There is a French book on him, I was interviewed, while he was still alive, years ago, there was a French biography. But he was like a guy with a master plan. I saw it. It was like Khrushchev and the five year plan. He had this whole thing mapped out and nothing was going to stand in his way. He as this quiet, self-effacing man who was like a bull. He had a will of iron. Never raised his voice. Always got what he wanted. If you can tame Milt Jackson and Kenny Clarke, you’re strong. And that’s exactly what he did. Until Milt’s dying day he had a lot of resentment about that whole experience, even though it made him a millionaire. But I think that’s, I’ll go on record as saying overall that’s the greatest small ensemble in jazz history as a unit over a period of years. That music will last forever and they’re sleeping on it and you don’t hear about it now but you will. Because I saw how it worked, I saw how John made it work, and I — the way he made the compromises he deliberately made musically to get that sound which were misunderstood and the other thing, and the whole thing. And his model was sort of Duke Ellington, the dignity, the whole thing, where he wanted the group to go. It’s an incredible story. I mean yes it should be, I’m sure it’s been written about a lot. But he was a powerful influence on me.
There’s a record, the last concert, there’s a moment on that record, a song called “One Never Knows”—

There you go. I don’t know, I can’t even describe, the middle of that piece is so sublime or something that — it’s like you said those people in the restaurant who would like pay attention when things went down. It’s like it’s so subtle but perfect.
